newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Horn slams Serb, Bulgarian hardline socialists.
newsitem.headline: Horn slams Serb, Bulgarian hardline socialists.

text.p: Hungary's Socialist Prime Minister Gyula Horn said on Monday the current wave of mass unrest in Serbia and Bulgaria was a result of the two socialist governments delaying democratic reforms.
"Parties (in Serbia and Bulgaria) which call themselves socialist have not carried out what international requirements demanded," Horn told a news conference.

"(The problems of both countries') democratic transformation and the normal operation of the system have not been solved, while in Bulgaria (social and economic) reforms have not yet even begun," he added.
Tens of thousands of people have been protesting in mass rallies in Belgrade and elsewhere in Serbia over the past two months against the manipulation of the results of local elections.
Bulgaria has also faced mass rallies and strikes since last year, as pressure grows on the ex-communist rulers to hold a general election almost two years ahead of schedule.
Horn said that the street protests now happening in Serbia and Bulgaria were equivalent to those which peacefully ended the decades of communist rule in Hungary seven years ago.

He said a sharp division must be made between socialist parties in those countries and the Hungarian socialists, who have been accepted into the worldwide Socialist International. The two Balkan parties have not.
The Hungarian Socialist Party, which regained power in 1994 elections, is the legal successor to the communist party the MSZMP, which ruled Hungary for decades.
The MSZMP was transformed into a social democratic-type grouping by reform communists including Horn at the end of the 1980s.
The Hungarian government, made up of Socialists and liberal Free Democrats, stressed its concerns over the situation in Serbia in a statement on Sunday.

"The government of the Hungarian Republic and the country's public views with growing concern the tension in Serbia over the manipulation of the November 1996 local elections' results," the statement said.
"Suggestions of crushing with violent, administrative methods the social movements representing justified demands, are unacceptable to Hungary," the statement said.
